subtype: Testing the excuse [Response]
passage:
Saturday night.
Skipped Shalini's birthday dinner. My message to her said: "So sorry, massive work deadline, and my stomach's been off, and the traffic to Andheri is insane on Saturdays." Three reasons. Very convincing. Then I did the thing I've been practising: I wrote the real reason in my notebook, the way I'd say it to myself. It was one line. "I didn't want to see her college friends, because they make me feel boring." Then I asked: if Shalini sent me my own message, would I believe it? No. I'd think, three excuses means none of them is the real one. Ugh. So tomorrow I'm calling her to say sorry, properly, and maybe tell her the true thing, gently.
Vasudha

qa.a: Three: a work deadline, an upset stomach, and the traffic to Andheri.

qa.q: How did Vasudha feel on writing down the real reason?
qa.a: Uncomfortable and a bit embarrassed, because the honest reason, feeling boring around the college friends, was short and unflattering.

qa.a: Writing the real reason and asking whether Vasudha would believe the same message from Shalini; it shows a stack of excuses up as a cover.

subtype: Facts instead of grief [Actor]

Thursday: At the funeral, Jomon stands very straight and explains the order of prayers to his younger cousins. He doesn't cry. His mother watches him, worried.
The next Sunday: Sorting his grandfather's things, Jomon finds the old fishing hat Appachan wore every monsoon. He picks it up, smells it, and suddenly he is sobbing, the kind of crying that comes from deep down. His mother holds him for a long time.

qa.a: The old fishing hat Appachan wore every monsoon.

qa.q: Why did Jomon talk about heart failure in such a flat voice?
qa.a: Thinking about facts kept the grief at arm's length; the pain was too big to feel yet.

qa.a: Stay with him, say he is sorry, and not push him either to feel or to stop talking facts; being there matters more than words.

qa.q: What is Jomon's mother feeling at the funeral?
qa.a: Worried, watching him stand so straight and not cry.

grounding: A teenager whose grandfather died recites medical facts in a flat voice, and the tears come days later.

subtype: Analysing a breakup like a case study [Actor]

subtype: Letting thinking and feeling share the table [Response]

subtype: Letting thinking and feeling share the table [Response]

subtype: Partner wants feelings and gets a lecture [Receiver]

subtype: Noticing the calm that rings hollow [Observer]

The next morning she messaged me a calm, tidy analysis: "The company over-hired, the market shifted, it's structural, not personal." All true. I can't know what's inside her, but the calm sounded hollow to me. So I didn't ask what it meant. I asked, "How does it feel, Gurleen?" She stopped. Then she said, "Like I got thrown out." And she cried. I stayed on the call. Afterwards she ordered some dal and rice.

qa.a: It invited the feeling instead of more analysis, letting Gurleen say she felt thrown out and cry.

qa.q: What was Gurleen feeling beneath her analysis?
qa.a: Hurt and rejected, as if she had been thrown out, which the rational talk was covering.
